scripts.text:
Why would a wasp lay its egg inside a cockroach’s egg case?

Because the cockroach eggs inside will feed her young. The mother is an ensign wasp, a small wasp that uses the egg cases of certain cockroaches, including American cockroaches.

She braces herself against the case and pushes a slender egg-laying organ through its tough covering to place one egg inside. When that egg hatches, the young wasp, called a larva, uses tiny jaws to cut through the shells of individual cockroach eggs. That one larva feeds on the dozen or more eggs inside the case.

The young wasp develops into an adult inside that same case, then cuts a small hole to get out.

An adult is only about a quarter of an inch long. To recognize it, look at the rear part of its body. It’s attached by a narrow stalk, and the wasp waves that rear part up and down like a little signal flag, giving the ensign wasp its name.

If you spot this ensign wasp in your home, it won’t sting or bite you. And although its young feed on cockroach eggs, seeing one isn’t proof of an active cockroach infestation.

Helping you understand pests. Deep Six Pest Control.

changes: Removed repeated explanations of egg laying and reassurance about stinging and biting.
Clarified the sequence from the mother's egg to the feeding larva and emerging adult.
Connected the flag-like movement directly to recognition and the wasp’s name.
Preserved the exact hook and outro, limited host claims to certain cockroaches, and retained the sighting-versus-infestation distinction.
